proof: For any feasible (h_j,z_j), put W=sum_j h_j^2 sinh^2(z_j^2/2), E=sum_j j^2 h_j z_j^2 and Bq=sum_j j^3 h_j z_j^(3/2). Then E≥r_tilde^2/epsilon^2 and Bq≤epsilon^(-3/2). If W=infinity the desired lower bound is immediate; otherwise the following Cauchy-Schwarz calculation applies by finite sums and limits.

Define T=(r_tilde^2 epsilon^(-1/2)/2)^2=(1-delta_epsilon)^4 epsilon^(-1/2)/4, which tends to infinity. Let L={j:z_j≤T j^2}. For j in L, j^2 h_j z_j^2≤T^(1/2) j^3 h_j z_j^(3/2). Consequently sum_L j^2 h_j z_j^2≤T^(1/2)epsilon^(-3/2)=r_tilde^2/(2epsilon^2). The complementary set H carries E_H≥r_tilde^2/(2epsilon^2).

Cauchy-Schwarz on H gives E_H^2≤W F_H, where F_H=sum_H j^4 z_j^4/sinh^2(z_j^2/2). For sufficiently small epsilon, T≥2. The scalar f(z)=z^4/sinh^2(z^2/2) decreases for z≥2: its logarithmic derivative is4/z-2z coth(z^2/2)<0. Also sinh(z^2/2)≥exp(z^2/2)/4 there. Since z_j>T j^2 on H, F_H≤16 T^4 sum_{j≥1} j^12 exp(-T^2 j^4)≤C0 T^4 exp(-T^2).

One explicit finite constant is C0=16·12!/(1-e^(-1))^13. Indeed for T≥1, exp[-T^2(j^4-1)]≤exp[-(j-1)] and j^12≤12! binom(j+11,12); the resulting generating series is (1-e^(-1))^(-13). All sums are nonnegative, so truncation/limit operations preserve these bounds.

Every feasible point therefore satisfies W≥r_tilde^4 exp(T^2)/(4 C0 epsilon^4 T^4). Taking its infimum and using the actual definition u_epsilon^2=2 inf W gives u_epsilon^2≥r_tilde^4 exp(T^2)/(2 C0 epsilon^4 T^4).

Here T^2=(1-delta_epsilon)^8 epsilon^(-1)/16. The last lower bound grows faster than every fixed power of epsilon^(-1). The displayed carrier asymptotic instead gives u_epsilon~c epsilon^(-13/4)epsilon^(7/8)=c epsilon^(-19/8), a fixed power, contradiction.
